title: TB Transmission and Control: Droplet Nuclei, Isolation Rooms, N95s and MAC Risk in HIV
summary: Learn how tuberculosis spreads in droplet nuclei, how often infection progresses with and without HIV, what an airborne infection isolation room and an N95 respirator must provide, and when disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis still applies in advanced HIV.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 59 Hit 1 (droplet nuclei; progression risk with and without HIV), Hit 10 (disseminated MAC in AIDS and prophylaxis) and Hit 14 (infection control: negative pressure, air changes, respirators). Checked against the CDC 2005 health-care TB transmission guideline (Jensen 2005), the CDC clinical overview pages on TB and latent TB infection, three reviews on progression risk with HIV (Gopalaswamy 2020, Migliori 2021, Pawlowski 2012), the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society NTM guideline (Dawood 2024) and To 2020. The US adult and adolescent opportunistic-infection guideline page on clinicalinfo.hiv.gov returned 403 to both a direct request and a page-fetch tool and was not read. Corrections: the reviewer gives droplet nuclei as 1–10 µm, but CDC gives about 1–5 µm; ≥6 ACH is the minimum only for older rooms, with ≥12 ACH for new construction or renovation; N95 respirators are certified at 0.3 µm, not for “1–5 µm particles”; the reviewer’s “prophylaxis at CD4 <50, stop at CD4 >100 for ≥3 months” is replaced in current guidance by no routine primary prophylaxis when ART is started promptly and stopping once ART is fully suppressive. The reviewer’s “12/hour for autopsy suites” is taught as CDC’s wording (autopsy settings should meet or exceed AII-room requirements). Prophylaxis doses are not taught. The Number Vault (table) is not fully taught and is not mapped.

objectives: Describe how M. tuberculosis is transmitted by droplet nuclei and how often infection progresses with and without HIV.
State the negative-pressure, air-change and exhaust requirements of an airborne infection isolation room.
Distinguish the role of an N95 respirator from that of a surgical mask in TB control.
Explain when primary prophylaxis against disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex applies in advanced HIV.

scenes.title: One cough, three decisions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: an adult with HIV, not on antiretroviral therapy, CD4 count 35 cells/µL, three weeks of cough; sputum AFB smear positive. Three cards: (1) Which room? (2) What does the nurse wear, and what does the patient wear on the way to radiology? (3) Besides tuberculosis, which mycobacterium threatens this patient, and is prophylaxis automatic? Question token: “Room, mask, and MAC?”

cues.text: An adult with HIV, not on antiretroviral therapy, has a CD4 count of thirty-five and three weeks of cough. The sputum smear is positive for acid-fast bacilli.
Which room does this patient need, and what should the nurse and the patient each wear?
And with a CD4 count this low, which other mycobacterium is a threat, and is prophylaxis automatic?

scenes.title: How tuberculosis travels and who progresses
scenes.altText: Schematic: a cough producing droplet nuclei that drift through a room into a second person’s alveoli. Card 1 (CDC 2005; CDC clinical overview): droplet nuclei are about 1–5 µm, generated when a person with pulmonary or laryngeal TB coughs, speaks, sneezes or sings; they can stay airborne for hours; M. tuberculosis spreads through air, not by surface contact; infection follows inhalation of droplet nuclei that reach the alveoli. Card 2 (CDC): without treatment about 5% of infected people develop TB disease in the first two years and another 5% later in life (about 5–10% lifetime). Card 3: HIV is a high-risk condition for progression; reviews estimate the yearly risk with HIV at about 7–10% (Gopalaswamy 2020), up to 10% (Migliori 2021) or 5–15% (Pawlowski 2012).

cues.text: Tuberculosis travels in droplet nuclei, tiny particles about one to five micrometres across, made when a person with lung or laryngeal tuberculosis coughs, speaks or sings.
They can stay in the air for hours. The bacteria spread through the air, not by touching surfaces, and infection starts when droplet nuclei reach the alveoli.
Most infected people never get sick. Without treatment, about five percent develop disease in the first two years, and another five percent later in life.
HIV changes that. It is one of the strongest risks for progression, and reviews put the yearly risk with HIV at roughly seven to ten percent, though estimates range from five to fifteen.

scenes.title: Airborne infection isolation and respirators
scenes.altText: AII room card (CDC 2005): single-patient room under negative pressure, so air flows from the corridor into the room (pressure differential ≥0.01 inch of water gauge, 2.5 Pa); ≥12 air changes per hour (ACH) for new construction or renovation; older rooms built under the pre-1994 guidance should have ≥6 ACH and be raised toward 12 when feasible; air exhausted outside or recirculated through HEPA filtration. Other negative-pressure areas: bronchoscopy suites, sputum-induction rooms, autopsy suites, clinical laboratories; autopsy settings should meet or exceed AII-room requirements. Respirator card: staff entering an AII room wear at least an N95 disposable respirator — certified ≥95% efficient at removing 0.3 µm particles, the size at which filters are generally least efficient — with fit testing. Surgical or procedure masks are designed to keep the wearer’s secretions out of the air, so the patient wears one during transport.

cues.text: A patient with suspected infectious tuberculosis goes into an airborne infection isolation room: a single room under negative pressure, so air flows from the corridor into the room, and is exhausted outside or through a HEPA filter.
New or renovated rooms should reach at least twelve air changes per hour. Six is the minimum only for older rooms, which should be raised toward twelve when feasible.
Bronchoscopy, sputum induction, laboratories and autopsy suites are also negative-pressure areas, and autopsy rooms should meet or exceed isolation-room standards.

Staff entering the room wear at least a fit-tested N95 respirator, certified to remove ninety-five percent of point-three micrometre particles. A surgical mask is different: it keeps the wearer’s secretions in, so the patient wears it during transport.

scenes.title: Disseminated MAC and when prophylaxis applies
scenes.altText: MAC card (Dawood 2024; To 2020): disseminated NTM disease in people with HIV is mostly Mycobacterium avium complex and occurs most often at CD4 counts <50 cells/µL, seldom above 100; without ART or prophylaxis, disseminated MAC affected about 20% of patients with CD4 <100. Prophylaxis card: routine primary prophylaxis is not recommended when ART is started promptly; it is reserved for patients not on fully suppressive ART (To 2020: CD4 <50 and not on fully suppressive ART) or, in the Southern African guideline, considered with a specialist for patients on salvage regimens; azithromycin is the agent of choice (weekly dosing), with clarithromycin or rifabutin as alternatives (exclude active TB before rifabutin); prophylaxis can stop once ART is fully suppressive (Dawood 2024: sustained viral-load suppression >3 months). Hook answers: (1) AII room; (2) nurse: fit-tested N95, patient: surgical mask in transit; (3) MAC is a risk at CD4 35, but starting ART promptly replaces routine prophylaxis.

cues.text: At very low CD4 counts, a second mycobacterium matters. Disseminated nontuberculous disease in HIV is mostly Mycobacterium avium complex, and it occurs most often below fifty CD4 cells per microlitre.

Current guidance no longer gives routine prophylaxis when antiretroviral therapy is started promptly. Prophylaxis is kept for patients who are not on fully suppressive therapy, with azithromycin as the usual choice and clarithromycin or rifabutin as alternatives.
Before rifabutin, active tuberculosis must be excluded. And once therapy fully suppresses the virus, prophylaxis can stop.

Back to the hook: an isolation room, an N95 for the nurse and a surgical mask for the patient in transit. And the low CD4 count is a reason to start antiretroviral therapy promptly, not automatic MAC prophylaxis.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A surgical mask protects the health-care worker from TB” (✓ staff need at least a fit-tested N95; the surgical mask is for the patient); “Six air changes per hour is the standard for every isolation room” (✓ ≥12 ACH for new or renovated rooms; 6 is the minimum for older rooms); “CD4 below 50 always means start MAC prophylaxis” (✓ not routinely when ART is started promptly; reserved for patients not on fully suppressive ART).

cues.text: Trap one: a surgical mask protects the nurse from tuberculosis. No: staff need at least a fit-tested N95. The surgical mask goes on the patient.
Trap two: six air changes per hour is the standard. No: new or renovated isolation rooms need at least twelve. Six is the floor for older rooms.
Trap three: a CD4 count below fifty always means MAC prophylaxis. No: if antiretroviral therapy starts promptly, routine prophylaxis is not recommended.

scenes.title: Small, sucked in, sealed out
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “SMALL, SUCKED IN, SEALED OUT, then ART FIRST.” Small = droplet nuclei about 1–5 µm; sucked in = negative pressure pulling corridor air into the room, ≥12 ACH; sealed out = a fit-tested N95 on staff, a surgical mask on the patient; ART first = at CD4 <50, prompt antiretroviral therapy rather than automatic MAC prophylaxis. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: small, sucked in, sealed out, then ART first. Small droplet nuclei. Air sucked into a negative-pressure room. Staff sealed behind a fit-tested N95. And at a CD4 below fifty, antiretroviral therapy first, not automatic MAC prophylaxis.

Where it breaks: droplet-nucleus sizes are approximate; the air-change and respirator rules are United States guidance, and older rooms may legally run at six; and MAC prophylaxis rules differ between guidelines and still apply to patients not on suppressive therapy.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Droplet nuclei ~1–5 µm · AII room: negative pressure, ≥12 ACH new · staff N95, patient surgical mask”, “Disseminated MAC mostly CD4 <50 · prompt ART replaces routine primary prophylaxis”.

cues.text: Tuberculosis spreads in droplet nuclei of about one to five micrometres, so suspected cases go into negative-pressure isolation rooms with at least twelve air changes per hour and staff wear fit-tested N95 respirators, while in advanced HIV prompt antiretroviral therapy now replaces routine Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis.

props.label: ~1–5 µm · negative pressure, ≥ 12 ACH · staff N95, patient mask
Disseminated MAC: CD4 < 50 · prompt ART, prophylaxis not routine

explanation.what: Plain language: tuberculosis spreads through the air in particles so small they float for hours, so a patient who may be infectious is put in a room that sucks air in rather than letting it out, and staff wear a tight-fitting respirator. Most infected people never get sick, but HIV makes progression far more likely, and people with very low CD4 counts are also at risk from another mycobacterium, MAC. Scientific terms: droplet nuclei, latent TB infection, progression, airborne infection isolation (AII) room, negative pressure, air changes per hour (ACH), HEPA filtration, N95 filtering-facepiece respirator, fit testing, surgical or procedure mask, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), primary prophylaxis, fully suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART).
explanation.why: Droplet nuclei (about 1–5 µm) stay airborne and reach the alveoli, so control relies on removing and containing room air (negative pressure, high air-change rates, exhaust or HEPA) and on respirators that filter fine particles. Cellular immunity holds latent infection in check; HIV weakens it, so progression to TB disease and dissemination of MAC both rise as CD4 counts fall. Restoring immunity with ART lowers MAC risk enough that routine prophylaxis is no longer needed when ART starts promptly.
explanation.measure: Droplet nuclei ~1–5 µm. Without treatment ~5% of infected people develop disease within 2 years and ~5% later. With HIV, reviews estimate ~7–10% per year (range 5–15%). AII room: negative pressure (≥0.01 inch water gauge, 2.5 Pa), ≥12 ACH new or renovated, ≥6 ACH older rooms (raise toward 12 when feasible), exhaust outside or HEPA. Staff: at least an N95 (≥95% efficient at 0.3 µm), fit tested. Disseminated MAC mostly at CD4 <50 cells/µL. Primary prophylaxis: not routine if ART starts promptly; azithromycin preferred, clarithromycin or rifabutin alternatives; stop once ART fully suppressive.
explanation.differs: N95 respirator (protects the wearer from inhaling droplet nuclei; fit tested) vs surgical or procedure mask (keeps the wearer’s secretions out of the air; for the patient). New or renovated AII rooms (≥12 ACH) vs older rooms (≥6 ACH). Latent infection (no disease, not infectious) vs TB disease. Older MAC rule (start at CD4 <50, stop at CD4 >100 for ≥3 months) vs current approach (prompt ART, prophylaxis only without fully suppressive ART).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the correct protective equipment for staff versus patient, the air-change rate or pressure direction of an isolation room, the droplet-nucleus size, the lifetime versus yearly progression risk, or the CD4 count at which disseminated MAC becomes likely. Older question banks may still use the CD4 >100 for 3 months rule for stopping MAC prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted to an airborne infection isolation room. Which protection is appropriate for the nurse entering the room?

options.text: At least a fit-tested N95 disposable respirator
options.rationale: Correct. CDC recommends at least an N95 respirator for health-care workers entering an AII room, with fit testing.
Incorrect. Surgical masks are designed to keep the wearer’s secretions out of the air; they are worn by the patient, not relied on to protect staff.

options.text: Gloves and gown only, because TB spreads by contact
options.rationale: Incorrect. M. tuberculosis spreads through the air, not by surface contact.

options.text: No protection if the door is kept closed
options.rationale: Incorrect. Room air contains droplet nuclei; staff entering need respiratory protection.

questions.stem: A hospital is building a new airborne infection isolation room. Which design meets the CDC 2005 recommendations?

options.text: Negative pressure relative to the corridor and at least 12 air changes per hour, exhausted outside or through HEPA
options.rationale: Correct. New construction or renovation should achieve ≥12 ACH, with negative pressure and outside exhaust or HEPA recirculation.

options.text: Positive pressure relative to the corridor and 12 air changes per hour
options.rationale: Incorrect. Positive pressure pushes contaminated air into the corridor; AII rooms are under negative pressure.

options.text: Negative pressure and 6 air changes per hour
options.rationale: Incorrect. Six ACH is the minimum for older rooms; new or renovated rooms should reach ≥12.

options.text: Neutral pressure with air recirculated to the ward without filtration
options.rationale: Incorrect. Air must be exhausted outside or recirculated through HEPA filtration.

questions.stem: An adult with newly diagnosed HIV has a CD4 count of 30 cells/µL, no signs of mycobacterial disease, and will start fully suppressive antiretroviral therapy this week. What is the current approach to disseminated MAC prevention?

options.text: Start ART promptly; routine primary MAC prophylaxis is not recommended
options.rationale: Correct. Current sources do not recommend routine primary prophylaxis when ART is started promptly.

options.text: Start azithromycin prophylaxis and continue until the CD4 count stays above 100/µL for 3 months
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is the older rule; prophylaxis is now reserved for patients not on fully suppressive ART.

options.text: Start rifabutin without excluding active tuberculosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Active TB must be excluded before rifabutin, and prophylaxis is not routine here.

options.text: No concern: disseminated MAC is seen only at CD4 counts above 200/µL
options.rationale: Incorrect. Disseminated MAC occurs most often at CD4 counts below 50 cells/µL.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 59 Hit 1 (and the figure caption and Number Vault) gives infectious droplet nuclei as 1–10 µm; the CDC 2005 guideline and the CDC clinical overview give about 1–5 µm. The lesson teaches 1–5 µm (register flag rv-tb-droplet-nuclei-size).

Ch. 59 Hit 1 gives the yearly risk of active TB with HIV as 7–10%. Gopalaswamy 2020 gives 7–10% per year, but Migliori 2021 gives up to 10% per year and Pawlowski 2012 gives 5–15% annually; the lesson presents the figure as a review estimate with a range (register flag rv-tb-hiv-annual-risk).

Ch. 59 Hit 14 gives “≥6 air changes/hour (12/hour for autopsy suites)”. CDC 2005 sets ≥12 ACH for new construction or renovation of AII rooms, with ≥6 ACH only for older rooms (to be raised toward 12 when feasible), and says autopsy settings should meet or exceed AII requirements (register flag rv-tb-aii-air-changes).

Ch. 59 Hit 14 describes respirators as “filtering 1–5 µm particles”. CDC 2005 describes the minimum, the N95, as ≥95% efficient at removing 0.3 µm particles (the size at which filters are generally least efficient), with fit testing (register flag rv-tb-respirator-filter-spec).

Ch. 59 Hit 10 says to give MAC prophylaxis at CD4 <50/µL and stop it once CD4 >100/µL for ≥3 months on ART. Dawood 2024 and To 2020 say routine primary prophylaxis is not recommended when ART is started promptly, and that prophylaxis can stop once ART is fully suppressive (Dawood 2024: sustained viral suppression >3 months). The US OI guideline page could not be read (403) (register flag rv-mac-prophylaxis-art).

The isolation-room, air-change and respirator rules taught here are United States CDC guidance (2005), and the MAC prophylaxis sources are a Southern African guideline and a review. Philippine infection-control and HIV guidelines are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.

verification.notes: 5 factual claims checked against the CDC 2005 guideline, two CDC clinical overview pages, three reviews on HIV progression risk, the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society NTM guideline and To 2020; 1 pending (autopsy 12/hour as a number; prophylaxis doses), not taught as facts. The US OI guideline page returned 403 and was not read. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
